**Short answer:** it can be worth it as a way to buy placements if you accept that they're paid links. It doesn't replace earned links, and I haven't verified its current pricing or catalog quality.

## What Serpzilla does

It's a self-serve marketplace of publisher sites that sell links. You browse sites, see each one's metrics and price, and order directly. Placements come in three forms:

- **Guest posts:** a new article on the publisher's site that links to you.
- **Insertions:** your link added to an existing page.
- **Monthly rented links:** you pay recurring fees, and the link disappears when you stop.

It also has an MCP server, so you can drive it from an AI agent. You pick each site and price yourself. A managed service like LinkDR does the sourcing and outreach for you instead.

## The main issue: these are paid links

Google's spam policy treats links bought to influence rankings as link spam. That covers followed links that pass ranking credit. Paid links are fine if they carry `rel="sponsored"` or `rel="nofollow"`. Marketplace links are often sold as followed, so the likely outcomes are:

- Google ignores the links.
- For a large or obvious pattern, you get a manual action.

Whether to buy is your call. This is the one risk warning I'll give.

## When it can be worth it

- You have budget but little time, and you want control over which sites you pay.
- You're after AI citations or referral traffic. A sponsored or nofollow placement on a page that AI engines already cite for your category can help, even without ranking credit.
- You vet each site individually.

## When to skip it or be careful

- Your page problem isn't authority. If the page is thin, mismatched to intent, or unindexed, links won't fix it. Run a page-level link gap against the pages that outrank you first.
- You'd rent links. They stop working when you stop paying.
- You'd buy sitewide or footer packages or exact-match anchors. Those are the easiest patterns to detect.

## How to use it if you do

1. Judge each site on topic fit, real organic traffic that isn't collapsing, and what else it links out to. Ignore the domain rating the marketplace shows.
2. Buy a few relevant placements instead of volume.
3. Use branded or plain anchors, and spread links across several pages instead of one commercial page.
4. Don't promise yourself a ranking lift.

Collaborator, WhitePress and Adsy are comparable marketplaces. Compare their catalogs for your language and niche.

Start with the free tactics. Unlinked mention reclamation, partner and integration pages, "best X" list inclusion, and directories usually give better quality per dollar. Buy placements only to fill a gap those leave.

# First 20 backlinks with no budget

Zero budget rules out paid placements, which is fine. Those are also the riskiest route under Google's spam policy. Everything below costs only time. I don't know your product or site yet, so this is the general sequence. The last section lists what I need to tailor it.

## Work in this order

**1. Take the links you're already owed (about 3-6 links, 1-2 hours each)**
- **Partners, customers, vendors, and integrations.** Ask for a link from any "customers", "partners", "integrations", or "powered by" page. Offer a short case study or quote in exchange. These are relevant, easy, and they come from people who already know you.
- **Unlinked mentions.** Set up Google Alerts for your brand and founder names. Search `"your brand" -site:yoursite.com`. Email the author and ask them to add a link.
- **Broken or moved links.** Check Search Console's Links report for links pointing at 404 pages. Redirect them, and ask the linker to update where it matters.

**2. Directories and launch sites (about 5-8 links, foundation only)**
Product Hunt, AlternativeTo, G2 and Capterra free listings, niche startup directories, and relevant "awesome" lists on GitHub. These links are low-value for ranking, but they give you a base profile and show up in AI answers. Use the **directory-submissions** skill for a vetted list and tracker.

**3. Expert and community participation (about 3-5 links)**
- **Journalist-request platforms with free tiers**, such as Connectively or Qwoted. Answer only the queries where you have real expertise.
- **Podcasts and newsletters** in your niche. Pitch your founder as a guest. Show notes usually carry a link.
- **Guest posts on editorial sites only**, with a branded or plain anchor in the bio. Avoid "write for us" farms.
- **Reddit, Slack, and forums.** Take part as yourself. You'll mostly get mentions rather than links, but those mentions feed AI citations.

**4. "Best X" list inclusion (about 3-5 links)**
Run your category's questions through ChatGPT and Perplexity and note which third-party listicles they cite. Email those authors and ask for an honest evaluation. This is the highest-value free tactic for AI visibility.

**5. One linkable asset, only if you have the time**
A free calculator, template, or original data point earns links on its own and gives your outreach something to point to. Don't start here, because it takes the longest.

## Rules to follow
- **Don't trade products or services for links** unless the link carries `rel="sponsored"` or `nofollow`. Google counts that as payment.
- **Don't join link-swap schemes or use automated link tools.**
- **Let linkers pick the anchor text.** Don't ask for keyword-rich anchors.
- **Send links to the pages that need them**, not only your homepage. Also add internal links from your strongest pages to your target page. That's free and often covers half the gap.

## Realistic expectations
Twenty links over 6-8 weeks is doable at 3-5 hours a week. Expect most of them to come from steps 1-2. Rankings lag by weeks to months, so track new referring domains, not positions, at first.

## What I need from you
1. Your site URL and what the product does.
2. The one or two pages that most need to rank.
3. What you could link to: data, a tool, integrations, customers, partners.
4. Hours per week, and whether anyone besides you can do outreach.
5. Any past link buying, swaps, or manual actions.

# First 20 backlinks on a zero budget

I don't know your product or site yet, so this is the generic path. Tell me what you sell and I'll turn it into a specific prospect list. Everything below is free and earned, so none of it falls under Google's paid-link rules.

## Order of attack

Work from easiest to hardest. The first three buckets can realistically get you to 12-15 links.

**1. Foundation links (target: 6-8, about a week)**
- Submit to startup, SaaS, and AI directories: Product Hunt, AlternativeTo, BetaList, relevant "awesome" lists on GitHub, and niche directories in your category. These are low authority but quick, and they make your domain look real. The `directory-submissions` skill has a tracker if you want it.
- Fill in every profile you control: LinkedIn company page, Crunchbase, GitHub, X, and the founders' personal sites and bios. Each one is a link.
- Create listings on review platforms such as G2 and Capterra. Free listings exist for most.

**2. Relationships you already have (target: 4-6, about a week)**
- **Customers:** ask for a case study, testimonial, or "powered by" mention on their site. Testimonials with a link-back are a common trade.
- **Partners, vendors, and integrations:** ask to be listed on their partner or integrations page. If you integrate with a tool, its marketplace usually links to you.
- **Investors, accelerators, and communities you belong to:** portfolio and member pages often link out.

**3. Reclamation (target: 3-5, ongoing)**
- Set up Google Alerts for your brand and founder names. Email anyone who mentions you without linking and ask them to add one.
- Open Search Console's Links report and check for links pointing to old or 404 URLs. Redirect those pages.

**4. One earned asset (target: 3-5, weeks 2-6)**
- Build one thing people cite: a free calculator, a template, a short original data post from your own product numbers, or a glossary of your category's terms.
- Don't add it to the pile of generic blog posts. Pitch it directly to people who maintain resource lists. Find those pages with a search like `"[your topic]" intitle:resources` or `inurl:tools`.

**5. Expert and community mentions (supplementary)**
- Answer journalist requests for free. Qwoted, Featured, and the free tiers of similar services work. The `public-relations` skill covers pitching.
- Guest on podcasts or write for editorial sites in your niche. Skip any "write for us" link farms.
- Take part in Reddit and community threads as yourself. These earn mentions more than links, but AI assistants often cite those threads.

## Rules that save you trouble
- Ask for the link and let the other person pick the anchor text. Branded or plain-URL anchors look natural.
- Point links at pages that need them, not only the homepage.
- Qualify each target for relevance and real traffic before you pitch. Twenty relevant links beat a hundred junk ones.
- Don't trade links in bulk, and don't use automated tools or link networks. They are the quickest way to a penalty.
- Add internal links from your strongest pages to your target pages. It costs nothing and often closes part of the gap.

## Realistic expectations
Expect 20 links in about 6-8 weeks if you spend 4-5 hours a week. Rankings lag links by weeks to months, so judge progress by referring domains, which you can see free in Search Console.

**Usually no.** Don't disavow just because Semrush marks links as toxic.

**Why not**
- Google has said for years that it ignores most spammy links automatically. Random scraper, directory, and foreign-language junk links are typically just discounted.
- Semrush's "toxicity score" is a third-party heuristic, not a Google signal. It flags many harmless links.
- Disavowing good or neutral links by mistake can remove value you were getting. The file is also easy to misuse and slow to undo.

**When disavowing is worth it**
- You have a **manual action** in Search Console for "unnatural links to your site."
- You (or a past agency) **bought links or ran link schemes**, and you can see a pattern, not just a few stray links.
- You're hit by a **large, obvious negative-SEO attack**, such as thousands of paid-looking links with exact-match anchors, and you see a matching ranking or traffic drop.

**What I'd do**
1. Check Search Console → Manual actions. If it's empty, you almost certainly don't need to disavow.
2. Compare the timing of any traffic drop against when the links appeared. If there's no correlation, leave them alone.
3. If you did build bad links yourself, first try to get them removed. Disavow only the ones that remain.
